title: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
summary: Why BitNet b1.58 uses weights in {-1, 0, +1}: absmean quantization, matmuls made of additions, training from scratch with the straight-through estimator, and packed CPU kernels.
outcomes: Explain why a ternary weight carries log2(3) = 1.58 bits and why the zero value matters
Compute absmean ternary weights and absmax INT8 activations for a small matrix and vector
Trace a ternary matrix-vector product as integer adds and subtracts with one rescale per output
Explain why training from scratch with latent weights and STE beats post-training quantization
Compute packed memory for a 2B ternary model and explain how I2_S, TL1 and TL2 kernels work

lessons.title: Why weight bytes set the price of decoding

blocks.md: In GPU and inference basics you saw that decoding one token reads every weight once, so the time per token has a floor of *weight bytes / memory bandwidth*. Weights are the bill. Take BitNet b1.58 2B4T, the model this course ends on. Its config (hidden size 2560, FFN size 6912, 30 layers, 5 KV heads of size 128) gives **2,084,044,800** weights inside linear layers, plus a 128,256 x 2560 embedding.

Stored as FP16 (2 bytes each), those linear weights are **4.17 GB**. At 1.58 bits each they would be **0.41 GB**. Since decode speed is roughly bandwidth divided by bytes read, cutting bits per weight raises the ceiling on tokens per second almost proportionally. Drag the bandwidth slider in the plot below to see the ceiling for a laptop (around 100 GB/s) versus a server GPU.

blocks.title: Decode ceiling vs bits per weight (2.08B linear weights)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: tokens/s = bandwidth / bytes read per token, ignoring KV cache, activations and compute. At 100 GB/s, FP16 weights cap decode near 24 tokens/s.
Ternary weights at 1.585 bits raise the same ceiling to about 242 tokens/s, roughly 10x, because every token reads 10x fewer bytes.
The catch: a 128,256 x 2560 output head kept in BF16 is 0.66 GB, more than all the ternary weights. With it the ceiling at 1.585 bits drops to about 93 tokens/s.
More bandwidth lifts every curve equally. The ratio between formats, not the absolute number, is what bits per weight buys.

blocks.md: The usual way to shrink weights is **post-training quantization (PTQ)**: train in full precision, then round the finished weights to fewer bits, sometimes with clever error correction (GPTQ, AWQ, QuIP). PTQ works well at 8 and 4 bits. Below that it falls apart.

blocks.prompt: The BitNet paper (Wang et al., 2023) applied PTQ methods to a 6.7B FP16 Transformer at 8, 4, 2 and 1 bits. Guess the validation perplexity (lower is better; the FP16 model scores 15.19) after rounding its weights to 1 bit with absmax quantization.
blocks.reveal: **3.5 x 10^23.** The model is destroyed. GPTQ at 2 bits reached 1032 and QuIP at 2 bits 70.43. Meanwhile **BitNet**, a model trained from scratch with 1-bit weights and 8-bit activations, scored **17.07**, close to the FP16 model's 15.19.

blocks.title: 6.7B models: average zero-shot accuracy (BitNet paper, Table 3)

scenes.caption: Reference points: random guessing averages 43.8 on these four tasks; the FP16 Transformer reaches 57.8.
Post-training quantization degrades smoothly at first (56.7 at 8 bits, 52.9 at 4 bits) then collapses: 49.0 at 2 bits and 44.6 at 1 bit, barely above random.
BitNet, trained with 1-bit weights from the start, scores 55.9. Same bit budget as the collapsed PTQ model, a completely different outcome.

blocks.md:
That gap is the whole idea of this course. Instead of compressing a model that was optimized for real-valued weights, **train the model with low-bit weights from the first step**, so the optimizer finds a solution that works inside the constraint. The line of work comes from Microsoft Research:

- **BitNet** (Oct 2023): binary weights in {-1, +1}, 8-bit activations, trained from scratch up to 30B parameters.
- **BitNet b1.58** (Feb 2024): ternary weights in {-1, 0, +1}; reported to match an FP16 LLaMA-style model of the same size and tokens from 3B parameters up.
- **BitNet b1.58 2B4T** (Apr 2025): the first open native 1-bit LLM at 2B scale, 4 trillion training tokens, with GPU and CPU (bitnet.cpp) kernels.
A 1.58-bit model is not a compressed full-precision model. It is a model whose weights were ternary during training, so nothing is lost when you ship the ternary weights.

blocks.question: Decode on a laptop is memory-bandwidth-bound. Which change gives the biggest speedup ceiling for the same model?
options: Doubling the number of CPU cores used for the matmuls
Storing weights in 2 bits instead of 16
Switching attention to a faster softmax implementation
Using FP32 accumulators instead of FP16
blocks.explain: When decode is bandwidth-bound, time per token is about bytes read divided by bandwidth. Going from 16 to 2 bits reads 8x fewer weight bytes. More cores help only when compute is the bottleneck, and softmax or accumulator changes do not reduce weight traffic.

blocks.question: Why does post-training quantization to 1 bit fail so badly while BitNet at 1 bit nearly matches FP16?
options: PTQ uses worse rounding rules than BitNet
BitNet keeps a hidden FP16 copy of the weights at inference
PTQ rounds weights that were optimized for real values; BitNet's optimizer chose weights that already work as 1-bit values
BitNet uses more parameters than the PTQ baseline
blocks.explain: The BitNet team's FAQ puts it directly: PTQ can only quantize weights around the full-precision values, which need not be where good low-precision solutions lie. Training with the quantizer in the loop lets the optimizer search among ternary solutions. At inference BitNet uses only the low-bit weights, and the compared models have the same size.

lessons.title: Ternary weights: log2(3), absmean and the power of zero

blocks.md: A weight that can take 3 values, each equally likely, carries $\log_2 3$ bits of information, because $k$ equally likely choices need $\log_2 k$ bits to name. Two bits name 4 things, one bit names 2, and 3 sits in between. That is where the name **b1.58** comes from.

blocks.caption: Five ternary weights have 243 combinations, which fit in one byte: 8/5 = 1.6 bits per weight, close to the 1.585 limit. Real kernels trade some of that density for simpler unpacking, as lesson 5 shows.

blocks.md: BitNet b1.58 turns a real-valued matrix $W$ (n x m) into ternary values with **absmean quantization**: divide by the mean absolute value $\gamma$, then round and clip to {-1, 0, +1}. A tiny $\epsilon$ avoids division by zero.

blocks.caption: The scale is one number per weight matrix (per tensor). The effective weight is gamma times the ternary value.

blocks.md: Let us run it on a toy 4 x 4 matrix. The 16 absolute values sum to 4.59, so $\gamma = 4.59 / 16 = 0.286875$. Anything with $|W/\gamma| < 0.5$ rounds to 0, which here means $|W| < 0.143$.

blocks.title: Absmean quantization of a toy 4 x 4 weight matrix

scenes.caption: Real-valued weights W. Mean absolute value gamma = 0.286875. Small entries like -0.07 and 0.03 carry little signal.
Divide by gamma. Now the threshold for keeping a weight is 0.5 in magnitude. Entries like 3.07 and -2.13 are far outside [-1, 1] and will be clipped.
Six entries have |W/gamma| below 0.5: -0.24, 0.10, 0.38, 0.17, -0.07 and 0.31. They will round to 0, switching off 6 of 16 weights.
RoundClip result: 6 zeros, 6 plus ones, 4 minus ones. Note 3.07 and 1.46 both became +1: clipping throws away magnitude above gamma.
Dequantized view gamma x ternary: every weight is now -0.287, 0 or +0.287. Mean absolute error versus W is 0.146, about half of gamma. A trained BitNet never sees W; it only ever used this version.

blocks.prompt: In a trained BitNet b1.58 checkpoint, what fraction of weights do you expect to be 0?
blocks.reveal: The team's FAQ reports the distribution of {-1, 0, +1} in checkpoints is **nearly uniform**, so roughly a third are zero, set by the absmean formula. They note you could raise the share of zeros by scaling gamma up, but preliminary experiments showed that hurt performance.

blocks.md: Why add 0 at all? The original BitNet used binary weights: $\widetilde{W} = \mathrm{Sign}(W - \alpha)$ with $\alpha$ the mean of $W$, and a scale $\beta$. Every input always pushes every output up or down. With a zero, a weight can ignore an input entirely, which the b1.58 paper calls **explicit feature filtering** and credits for stronger modeling. The FAQ adds what else was tried: {-1, +1} scaled well but was weaker, especially at small sizes; {0, 1} was unstable and diverged early; 5 levels {-2, ..., 2} were unnecessary since ternary already matched full precision.

"1-bit LLM" is the family name, not the bit count. BitNet b1.58 weights are ternary (about 1.58 bits), the original BitNet was binary (1 bit), and in both the activations are 8-bit and the embeddings stay in higher precision.

Why the mean and not the max? An absmax scale would be set by the single largest weight, so most weights would fall below half of it and round to 0. The mean tracks the typical weight, giving a useful mix of zeros and plus or minus ones.

blocks.question: A weight matrix has gamma = 0.4. Which ternary values do the weights [0.5, -0.1, -0.9, 0.19] get?
blocks.explain: Divide by gamma: [1.25, -0.25, -2.25, 0.475]. Round: [1, 0, -2, 0], then clip -2 to -1. Note 0.475 is just under the 0.5 threshold, so 0.19 is switched off even though it is not tiny.

blocks.question: You pack 5 ternary weights per byte. How many bits per weight is that, and how far is it from the information limit?
options: 1.6 bits, about 0.015 bits above log2(3)
1.58 bits, exactly the limit
2 bits, since each weight needs a 2-bit code
1.67 bits, because 3 weights need 5 bits
blocks.explain: 3^5 = 243 fits in 256 codes, so 8 bits hold 5 weights: 8/5 = 1.6 bits each, versus log2(3) = 1.585. 2 bits is what simple per-weight codes use, and 1.67 (5 bits per 3 weights) is bitnet.cpp's TL2 layout, which trades density for fast lookups.

lessons.title: BitLinear: a matrix multiply made of additions

blocks.md: BitNet replaces every `nn.Linear` in attention and the FFN with a **BitLinear** layer. Inside it, weights are ternary and activations are 8-bit integers (W1.58A8). Activations are quantized with **absmax** per token: scale the vector so its largest magnitude maps to 127, then round. This is the official training code's formula.

blocks.caption: Both scales sit outside the integer product, so they are applied once per output, not once per weight.

scenes.caption: Activations arrive in BF16. A normalization (SubLN; RMSNorm in the official code) keeps their variance stable, which the BitNet paper adds specifically so quantized outputs keep a sane scale.
Each token's vector is scaled so its max magnitude is 127 and rounded to INT8. The scale s is kept for later.
The core: ternary weights times INT8 activations. Every product is +v, -v or nothing, so the inner loop is integer additions and subtractions.
One multiply per output undoes both scales: y = (gamma / s) x integer sum. Apart from the normalization and the absmax step, that is the only floating-point arithmetic in the layer.

blocks.md: Now a concrete pass. Use the ternary matrix from lesson 2 (gamma = 0.286875) and the activation vector x = [1.31, -0.4, 2.6, 0.7]. The max magnitude is 2.6, so s = 127 / 2.6 = 48.846.

blocks.title: Absmax INT8 quantization of one token

scenes.caption: The token's activations. The largest magnitude, 2.6 at index 2, sets the scale.
Multiply by s = 48.846. The max lands exactly on 127; the rest scale proportionally.
Round to integers. Worst rounding error here is 0.46 of one step out of 127, under 0.4% of the range.

blocks.title: Ternary matrix-vector product with no multiplies
blocks.code:
W = [[ 1, 0, 1,-1],
     [ 0, 1,-1, 0],
     [-1, 0, 1, 0],
     [ 1,-1, 1, 0]]      # ternary weights
xq = [64, -20, 127, 34]  # int8 activations
gamma, s = 0.286875, 48.846
y = []
for row in W:
    acc = 0                  # integer accumulator
    for w, v in zip(row, xq):
        if w == 1:
            acc += v
        elif w == -1:
            acc -= v
        # w == 0: skip, no work
    y.append(acc * gamma / s)  # one multiply per output

scenes.caption: Row 0 of W is [1, 0, 1, -1]. Start an integer accumulator at 0.
Weight +1 times 64: just add 64.
Weight 0: skip the input entirely. This is the feature filtering the zero buys.
Weight +1 times 127: add.
Weight -1 times 34: subtract. Row 0's integer sum is 157, from two adds and one subtract.
The other rows the same way: -20 - 127 = -147, -64 + 127 = 63, 64 + 20 + 127 = 211. 10 add or subtract steps in total, 4 multiplies.

blocks.prompt: The full-precision answer W x with the original real weights is [0.541, -0.990, 0.040, 2.164]. The ternary result is [0.922, -0.863, 0.370, 1.239]. Which step caused most of the gap: INT8 activations or ternary weights?
blocks.reveal: **Ternary weights.** Using the ternary W with the unquantized x gives [0.921, -0.861, 0.370, 1.236], almost identical to the INT8 result, so the 8-bit activations cost almost nothing. The large error comes from rounding a matrix that was never trained to be ternary. That is post-training quantization in miniature. A trained BitNet has no such gap because its real-valued weights never existed at inference: the network learned to compute with the ternary ones.

blocks.md: Why does avoiding multiplies matter? Using the energy model the BitNet papers cite (Horowitz, ISSCC 2014, with 7 nm figures via Zhang et al., 2022), at a 7 nm process an FP16 multiply costs 0.34 pJ and an FP16 add 0.16 pJ, while an INT8 add costs 0.007 pJ. One FP16 multiply-accumulate is 0.50 pJ against 0.007 pJ for the ternary add: a ratio of **71.4x**, which is the figure the b1.58 paper reports for matmul arithmetic energy.

blocks.title: Arithmetic energy per operation at 7 nm (pJ)

scenes.caption: An FP16 weight times an activation needs a multiply (0.34 pJ) and an add into the running sum (0.16 pJ).

A ternary weight needs only an INT8 add or subtract: 0.007 pJ, a sliver on this scale. 0.50 / 0.007 = 71.4x. This is arithmetic only; it ignores the energy of moving data, which shrinks too but separately.

blocks.md: "Matmul becomes additions" applies to the weight matrices. Attention scores (Q times K, then weights times V) multiply activations by activations, so they are not ternary. And the speedup only appears with a kernel that actually exploits ternary weights, which lesson 5 covers.

blocks.question: A ternary weight row has 1000 entries, 350 of them zero. Roughly what arithmetic does one output need?
options: 1000 multiplies and 999 adds
650 integer adds or subtracts, then 1 multiply by the combined scale
350 integer adds and 650 multiplies
650 multiplies, since zeros are skipped
blocks.explain: Each +1 adds the activation, each -1 subtracts it, each 0 is skipped: about 650 integer add or subtract steps. The scales gamma and s are shared, so they are applied once to the final sum.

blocks.question: A teammate implements BitLinear by computing gamma / s and multiplying it into every activation before the ternary matmul. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, it is mathematically identical and just as fast
It changes the result because gamma is per row
The activations become non-integer, so the inner loop needs floating-point arithmetic again, losing the INT8 add advantage
It double-counts gamma
blocks.explain: Scales are pulled outside the sum so the inner loop stays on small integers. Pre-multiplying makes every activation a float, so the adds become float adds. The math is equal in exact arithmetic, but the efficiency argument disappears. The official inference code applies both scales after the low-bit GEMM.

lessons.title: Training from scratch: latent weights and the STE

blocks.md: Training with ternary weights has an obvious problem. RoundClip is a staircase: flat almost everywhere, with jumps. Its derivative is 0 wherever it exists, so backpropagation through it would send zero gradient to every weight and nothing would learn.

The fix BitNet uses is the **straight-through estimator (STE)**, studied by Bengio, Leonard and Courville (2013), the reference BitNet cites: use the quantizer in the forward pass, but in the backward pass pretend it was the identity and pass the gradient straight through. To have something to pass it to, training keeps a full-precision **latent weight** for every parameter. The ternary weight is recomputed from the latent one on every forward pass.

blocks.title: Forward quantizer vs the gradient STE pretends it has

scenes.caption: Forward pass: the latent weight is snapped to -gamma, 0 or +gamma. The flat steps have zero slope, so the true gradient is useless.
Backward pass: STE treats the staircase as the line y = w, slope 1, so the loss gradient reaches the latent weight unchanged.
gamma is recomputed from the weights each step. A smaller gamma narrows the zero band (|w| < gamma / 2) and lowers the step height.

blocks.md: The official training code implements STE with a one-line trick. `w + (q(w) - w).detach()` evaluates to `q(w)` in the forward pass, but `detach()` hides the difference from autograd, so the gradient with respect to `w` is exactly 1.

blocks.code:
def weight_quant(w):
    scale = 1.0 / w.abs().mean().clamp_(min=1e-5)
    return (w * scale).round().clamp_(-1, 1) / scale

def activation_quant(x):
    scale = 127.0 / x.abs().max(dim=-1, keepdim=True).values.clamp_(min=1e-5)
    return (x * scale).round().clamp_(-128, 127) / scale

class BitLinear(nn.Linear):          # training version
    def forward(self, x):
        w = self.weight                # latent full-precision weights
        x_norm = RMSNorm(x)
        # straight-through estimator via detach()
        x_quant = x_norm + (activation_quant(x_norm) - x_norm).detach()
        w_quant = w + (weight_quant(w) - w).detach()
        return F.linear(x_quant, w_quant)
blocks.caption: Condensed from the BitNet team's official PyTorch BitLinear (Training Tips, Code and FAQ). Optimizer states and latent weights stay in high precision.

blocks.title: One training step with latent weights

nodes.label:
Ship: ternary W
plus one gamma

scenes.caption: Every step starts from the latent weights, which accumulate tiny updates in high precision.
Forward: ternarize on the fly and run the network exactly as it will run at inference.
Backward: the gradient passes straight through the quantizer and the optimizer updates the latent weights.
After training the latent weights are discarded. Only the ternary values and the per-matrix scale ship; they are what the network was trained with.

blocks.md: A latent weight can move for many steps without its ternary value changing. Here is a simplified trace: one latent weight starting at 0.30, a gradient that nudges it down by 0.03 per step, and gamma held fixed at 0.5 (in reality gamma drifts as all weights move).

blocks.title: A latent weight drifting until its ternary value flips

scenes.caption: Start: 0.30 / 0.5 = 0.60 rounds to +1.
One update later the latent weight is 0.27 (ratio 0.54). The ternary weight is still +1: the forward pass saw no change at all.
At 0.24 the ratio 0.48 drops below 0.5 and the weight flips to 0. Only now does the model's behavior change.
It stays 0 until the latent weight falls below -0.25. The magnitude of the latent weight acts like a confidence score for the ternary value.

blocks.md:
That picture explains the training recipe the BitNet team reports:

- **Large learning rate.** Small updates often change no ternary weight, so the original BitNet found a larger learning rate the simplest fix; BitNet trained stably at learning rates where the FP16 Transformer diverged. For b1.58 at 700M they used a peak of 1.5e-3 versus 2.5e-4 for the LLaMA baseline.
- **Two-stage schedule.** Decay the learning rate abruptly midway; the loss drops sharply there. Their 1-bit loss curves are S-shaped, so early checkpoints underpredict the final result.
- **Weight decay 0.1, then 0.** Weight decay shrinks latent weights, lowering their confidence and making ternary values flip more often, so it is switched off in the second stage.

Training a BitNet is not cheaper than training an FP16 model with today's code. Latent weights, gradients and optimizer states are high precision, and the FAQ notes their training ran in FP16/BF16 with no speedup. The savings are at inference.

This is the difference between **quantization-aware training from scratch** and **post-training quantization**. The FAQ adds that they tried continuing training from a 1-bit PTQ checkpoint and saw no improvement over training from scratch. The 2B4T report shows the payoff at 2B scale against INT4 PTQ of a strong model.

blocks.title: 2B4T vs Qwen2.5 1.5B in BF16 and INT4 PTQ (2B4T report, Table 2)

scenes.caption: Non-embedding memory in GB: 2.6 in BF16, 0.7 after INT4 PTQ, 0.4 for the native ternary model.
Average of MMLU, GSM8K and IFEval: 55.72 for BF16, 52.15 and 51.17 after INT4 PTQ, 55.01 for BitNet. PTQ lost about 3.5 to 4.5 points; BitNet sits near the BF16 model with the least memory.

blocks.question: Halfway through training, the BitNet b1.58 recipe sets weight decay to 0. Why does that help a ternary model in particular?
options: Weight decay would push ternary values toward 2
Weight decay shrinks latent weights toward the rounding threshold, so ternary values keep flipping; removing it lets them settle
Weight decay is incompatible with the STE gradient
It saves optimizer memory
blocks.explain: The latent weight's magnitude acts as confidence in its ternary value. Decay keeps pulling magnitudes down toward the |w| < gamma/2 band, causing frequent flips. With decay off and a lower learning rate, the ternary weights can converge.

blocks.question: What does the straight-through estimator do in BitLinear?
options: It computes the exact gradient of RoundClip
It skips the quantizer in the forward pass during training
It uses the quantized weights in the forward pass and treats the quantizer as identity in the backward pass
It quantizes the gradients to ternary values
blocks.explain: Forward uses w_quant so the loss reflects the ternary network; the detach() trick makes d(w_quant)/dw equal to 1, so gradients flow to the latent weights. The exact gradient of rounding is zero almost everywhere, and gradients stay high precision.

lessons.title: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers

blocks.md: No CPU or GPU has a native ternary type, so packing and the kernel decide whether the theory turns into speed. The 2B4T GPU kernel stores **four ternary values in one int8** in HBM, loads them into shared memory, unpacks and computes ('pack-store-load-unpack-compute'). On CPUs, **bitnet.cpp** (built on llama.cpp) offers three kernels.

**I2_S** maps each weight to a 2-bit code offline: -1 to `00`, 0 to `01`, +1 to `10`. At run time it unpacks and does an ordinary multiply-then-add with the INT8 activations. Simple, 2 bits per weight, and the paper recommends it with enough threads.

blocks.title: I2_S: four ternary weights become one byte

scenes.caption: Row 0 of our toy matrix: four ternary weights.
Each weight gets a 2-bit code: +1 is 10, 0 is 01, -1 is 00. Code 11 is never used, which is why 2 bits per weight wastes about 0.4 bits.

Four codes fill one byte. Simplified: the real layout interleaves codes across rows to suit SIMD loads. For 2B4T, 2,084,044,800 weights pack into 521,011,200 bytes, matching the U8 tensor size in the released checkpoint.

blocks.md: **TL1 and TL2** remove the multiply-add altogether with lookup tables (an idea from T-MAC and LUT-GEMM). For a pair of weights there are only $3^2 = 9$ possible patterns. So for each pair of activations, precompute all 9 signed sums once, then each pair of weights becomes a 4-bit index into that table.

blocks.caption: This matches the TL1 table in the bitnet.cpp report: (-1,-1) is index 0 and (+1,+1) is index 8.

blocks.title: TL1: two lookups replace the row-0 dot product

scenes.caption: With x_q = [64, -20, 127, 34], precompute all 9 sums for (x0, x1) = (64, -20). Index 0 is -64 + 20 = -44; index 8 is 64 - 20 = 44. This is done once per token and reused by every output row.
Same for (x2, x3) = (127, 34). Now each output row needs no arithmetic per weight, only lookups and adds.
Row 0 weights (+1, 0) give index 3 x 2 + 1 = 7: look up 64.
Weights (+1, -1) give index 3 x 2 + 0 = 6: look up 93. 64 + 93 = 157, the same integer sum as the add/subtract loop, with one lookup-and-add per weight pair instead of one operation per weight.

blocks.md: **TL2** groups three weights: 27 patterns. Half of them are negatives of the other half (the pattern (-1,0,1) gives minus the sum of (1,0,-1)), so the table only needs 14 entries (13 mirror pairs plus all zeros) and a separate **sign bit** says whether to negate. Three weights then cost a 4-bit index plus 1 sign bit: 5 bits for 3 weights, **1.67 bits per weight**, which the report says shrinks the model by 1/6 compared with TL1. The 14 entries fit a 16-entry SIMD shuffle (16 x int8 = 128 bits for AVX2 `vpshufb`), which is why groups of 3 is the limit.

blocks.title: Memory for 2B4T's 2.08B linear weights by format

scenes.caption: Computed from the config: 2,084,044,800 weights x bits / 8. FP16 is 4.17 GB, INT4 1.04 GB.
2-bit packing gives 0.52 GB, TL2 0.43 GB, and the information limit 0.41 GB. The report quotes 0.4 GB of non-embedding memory.

Now the surprise: the 128,256 x 2560 embedding in BF16 is 0.66 GB, bigger than every ternary weight combined. Total parameters are about 2.41B, which is why the bitnet.cpp README lists the model as 2.4B.

blocks.md:
Reported results (measured by the authors, not re-run here):

- **2B4T vs similar open models** (2B4T report, Table 1): 0.4 GB non-embedding memory vs 2.6 GB for Qwen2.5 1.5B; CPU decode latency 29 ms per token vs 65 ms; estimated decode energy 0.028 J vs 0.347 J; average benchmark score 54.19 vs 55.23.
- **b1.58 on GPU** (2024 paper, 2-bit Ladder kernel): at 3B, 2.71x faster decoding and 3.55x less memory than LLaMA 3B; at 70B on two A100s, 11x the batch size and 8.9x the throughput.
- **bitnet.cpp vs llama.cpp FP16** (CPU report, on test models of various sizes): 1.37x to 5.07x faster on an Apple M2 Ultra, 2.37x to 6.17x on an Intel i7-13700H, 55.4% to 82.2% less energy, and a 100B ternary model at 5 to 7 tokens per second on one CPU.

bitnet.cpp's kernels are **lossless**: they reproduce the training-time quantization exactly. On 1,000 prompts with a 700M BitNet b1.58 model, I2_S, TL1 and TL2 matched an FP32 reference token for token 100% of the time, versus 1.4% for llama.cpp's TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, which quantize activations in 256-element blocks unlike training.
Loading the 2B4T checkpoint in Hugging Face `transformers` saves memory but gives no speed or energy gain; the model card says the efficiency needs the dedicated bitnet.cpp kernels.

Tradeoffs and open problems:

- **You must pretrain.** The gains come from training ternary from scratch, so an existing FP16 model cannot simply be converted without loss.
- **Activations are still 8-bit.** BitNet a4.8 pushes inputs to attention and FFN to 4 bits and sparsifies intermediate states, activating 55% of parameters and supporting a 3-bit KV cache.
- **Not everything is ternary.** Embeddings, the output head, norms and attention math stay higher precision.
- **Hardware.** The 2B4T report notes commodity GPUs are not designed for 1-bit models and calls for hardware co-design.
- **Scale.** 2B4T has 2B parameters and a 4,096-token context; the report lists larger models and longer context as future work.

blocks.question: Why can TL2 store three ternary weights in 5 bits while TL1 needs 4 bits for two?
options: TL2 drops the zero value
TL2 uses mirror symmetry: 27 patterns become 14 unsigned table entries plus a 1-bit sign, so a 4-bit index plus a sign bit covers three weights
TL2 compresses the activations instead of the weights
TL2 uses 5 bits per weight
blocks.explain: Negating all three weights negates the sum, so only half the patterns need table entries (14, including all zeros). A 4-bit index picks the entry and a sign bit flips it. 5 bits / 3 weights = 1.67 bits per weight, versus 4/2 = 2 for TL1.

blocks.question: After packing 2B4T's linear weights into 2 bits, which part of the model is now the largest single block of weights?
options: The attention Q and K projections
The FFN weights, still 2.08 GB
The BF16 embedding and tied output head, about 0.66 GB
The RMSNorm parameters
blocks.explain: The 128,256 x 2560 embedding is 328M parameters at 2 bytes: 0.66 GB, versus 0.52 GB for all 2.08B ternary weights. Because the embeddings are tied, the output head reads that matrix every token, which is why large vocabularies matter more once the rest is ternary.
